lesson.title: Beyond Request and Response: Keeping the Line Open with WebSocket
lesson.summary: WebSocket upgrades a single HTTP connection into a persistent, full-duplex channel where either side can send messages at any time, which is a fundamentally different communication pattern from HTTP's request and response model.
lesson.body:
Ordinary HTTP, and RESTful APIs built on it, follow a strict pattern: the client sends a request, and the server sends back exactly one response. The server can never speak first. If a client needs to know about something new happening on the server, like a new chat message arriving or a stock price changing, its only option under plain HTTP is to keep asking, over and over, a technique called polling. Polling wastes requests when nothing has changed and adds latency when something has, because the client only finds out at its next scheduled check rather than the moment the event actually happens.

WebSocket exists to remove that limitation. A WebSocket connection begins as a normal HTTP request, carrying an Upgrade header asking to switch protocols, and if the server agrees it responds with a 101 Switching Protocols status. At that point the connection stops behaving like HTTP entirely and becomes a raw, persistent, full duplex channel, addressed with the ws or wss scheme. Full duplex means both sides can send messages independently and at any time, not just in response to something the other side sent. The server can push a new chat message to the client the instant it exists, and the client can send a message back a moment later, all over the same long lived connection, without either side having to open a new connection or wait for a request to be sent first.

It helps to be clear about how different this is from REST, which was just covered. REST is resource oriented and stateless: each request names a resource, carries everything the server needs to handle it, and the connection underneath is not something the API design cares about. WebSocket throws out the resource and request idea almost entirely. Once the handshake finishes, there are no more URLs or HTTP methods involved, just a stream of messages flowing in either direction over one connection that both sides keep open, often for as long as a user has a page open or an app running.

A live chat application is the clearest illustration. Under a polling approach, a client might send an HTTP GET every few seconds asking whether any new messages exist, meaning a message sent right after a poll could sit unseen for several seconds until the next poll happens, and most of those polls return nothing new at all. Under WebSocket, the client opens one connection when it joins the chat, and from then on the server simply sends a message down that connection the instant someone else posts one, with no request needed to trigger it, and the client can send its own messages up the same connection whenever the user types something. The result is lower latency and far less wasted traffic, which is exactly why WebSocket has become the standard choice for chat systems, live notifications, multiplayer games, and collaborative editing tools.
